title: State of the Art of DORA Metrics & AI Integration • Nathen Harvey & Charles Humble

segments.text: [music]
Welcome to the GoTo Podcast. Each
episode covers the brightest and boldest
[music] ideas from the world&#39;s leading
experts in software development. Tune in
for practical lessons, compelling
theories, and plenty [music] of
inspiration.
Go to gathers the brightest minds in the
[music] software community to help
developers tackle projects today, plan
for tomorrow, and create a better
future. Stay up tod date with the latest
in [music] tech through GOTO&#39;s toprated

YouTube channel [music] where you can

talks. Learn more at gotopia.te.
[music]
Hello and welcome to this new miniseries
for go to unscripted called the
state-of-the-art. This series will
explore generative AI of course, but
also other emerging trends in platform
engineering and security, new practices
and new programming languages. I&#39;m
Charles Humble. I have about 30 years
experience as a programmer architect and
CTO. And I&#39;m currently working mainly as
a freelance consultant, tech journalist,
editor, and podcaster. I&#39;ve just
published a book for the new stack
called Kubernetes at the edge. And I
mentioned this because during the course
of writing it, I found myself reflecting
on the fact that during my career, I&#39;ve
seen I&#39;m going to say five major shifts
in how enterprise software is built and
deployed. So the first was the adoption
of higher level languages, things like
Java and C and Visual Basic. The second
would be the agile movement. Then we had
public cloud, then DevOps and
particularly continuous delivery and
also microservices. And each of those
ultimately succeeded because I would
argue they reduced time to value. That&#39;s
to say, they enable someone in a
business to go from having an idea to
getting that idea in front of a customer
faster and at a lower cost. That
combination allows businesses to try
more ideas and use the market&#39;s response
to determine which ones resonate and
which ones don&#39;t. For all the hype and
excitement, it remains to be seen
whether generative AI will turn out to
be a sixth, though many people are
already persuaded that it is. Generative
AI certainly holds out the promise of
being able to write software faster. But
if that&#39;s true, how do we avoid
unintended consequences? And is that
solving a problem we actually have? My
[snorts] guest today, Nathan Harvey, is
someone who has thought deeply about
this topic. Nathan leads the Dora team
at Google Cloud, where he guides
organizations in optimizing their
software delivery. He leverages Dora&#39;s
extensive research to help teams enhance
developer experience and improve the
speed, stability, and efficiency of
their software delivery. Nathan is also
dedicated to fostering the growth of
technical communities such as the Dora
community of practice and has
co-authored several influential Dora
reports and contributed to the O&#39;Reilly
book 97 things every cloud near should
know. He and I met up recently in London
at the AI for the rest of us conference
where he gave a fantastic keynote called
Navigating the Generative AI revolution
in software development. Assuming the
video of that is out, we&#39;ll link to it
in the show notes. But that along with
the Dora research that underpins it is
kind of the underlying theme for this
show today. Nathan, welcome to the show.
&gt;&gt; Thanks so much, Charles. It&#39;s really
good to see you and and it was great to
see you in London a few weeks back.
&gt;&gt; Thank you. Yeah, lovely to see you as
well. So despite my ridiculously long
introduction, I managed to get all the
way to the end of it without actually
explaining what Dora is. So I&#39;m
imagining our our listeners and watchers
have have some idea, but can you give me
your kind of description what is Dora?
&gt;&gt; Yeah, for sure. Dora is a research
program that&#39;s been running for well
over a decade now. I think we&#39;re up to
12 or 13 years, something along those
lines. And this research really looks
into sort of the metrics and the
capabilities and conditions that teams
need to really understand how are they
doing with software delivery performance
and and probably more important than how
they&#39;re doing. What what things can they
do to improve that software delivery
performance? And as you said, software
delivery performance is sort of it&#39;s
sort of this this the crux of being able
to deliver software to your users so
that you can test out is is this a
feature that our customers want that the
market wants. And the more we&#39;re able to
ship features, the more we&#39;re able to
ship change, the better off we are in
terms of being able to make decisions
about what&#39;s the right thing to do for
our customers and for our users. So this
research program each year runs an
annual survey. This survey is an
anonymous survey that goes out to
organizations around the world. Uh, and
we&#39;re we&#39;re very lucky to get responses
from organizations of every shape and
size in every industry vertical. In
fact, in 2025, we received nearly 5,000
survey responses to our survey. We
complement this survey data with some
qualitative data as well. So, in
addition to having these 5,000 or so
survey responses, we also had about a
100 hours worth of qualitative data
interviews that our qualitative
researchers did one-on-one with
practitioners, with leaders, and so
forth. Now, the participants of this
survey and of our research program, many
of them are developers of some sort,
certainly technical practitioners,
whether that&#39;s someone who identifies as
a DevOps engineer or a software
engineer, like kind of across the board.
But we also hear from folks like product
managers, team leads, engineering
managers, CTO&#39;s, leadership and so
forth. So it&#39;s a pretty broad
perspective that we get each year which
really helps inform that research.
&gt;&gt; How did you get involved in Dora? What
was your kind of starting point for
that?
&gt;&gt; Sure. My starting point actually at when
the research program first launched, it
launched out of a company at the time
was called Puppet Labs and they ran the
first ever state of DevOps survey. At
the time I was a practitioner. I was
working in in an organization where we
were, you know, starting to adopt DevOps
practices. We were moving from the data
center into the cloud. I was leading a a
web operations team. And so I
participated in the first survey. And so
in that way I like to say that I&#39;ve been
involved since the very beginning. A few
years on I joined a company called Chef
where some of the lead researchers in
particular Dr. Nicole Forsrren and Jez
Humble were both working at the same
time that I was working at Chef. Uh
while they were there they were
continuing this store research program.
They eventually left Chef and then
founded a company called Dora. I stayed
at Chef until I joined Google, which
shortly after I joined actually acquired
Dora. So Nicole and Jez and I got to
work together again. They&#39;ve all since
moved on to other things and I&#39;ve taken
over leading the DORA program for the
last four or five years or so.
&gt;&gt; So I guess a question that comes up for
me is how neutral the research actually
is. So obviously this is now a Google
project. Google has Google Cloud and I&#39;m
aware you know you obviously I read the
reports every year you don&#39;t promote
Google cloud but Google has also been
pushing AI very heavily and is kind of
an AI first company in many respects I
mean I would perhaps say that they were
one of the first companies to to to
really sort of invest in AI as a as a
set of technologies so given all of that
how much does Google&#39;s corporate agenda
influ influence what Dora covers what it
writes about if at all.
&gt;&gt; Yeah, that&#39;s a it&#39;s a completely fair
question. I would say first and foremost
that the research has always been
program and platform agnostic. We aren&#39;t
asking about specific technologies, but
we are asking about those capabilities
and conditions that high performing
teams have. Now, of course, I&#39;m employed
by Google as are the researchers and a a
large number of people that are
contributing to Dora, but we we don&#39;t we
we do sort of maintain a a fair bit of
independence in terms of what we
research and so forth. Dora has always
been very interested in understanding
what are the trends within industry and
really trying to spot those trends and
follow them as they evolve. as an
example, you know, Dora started right at
the early stages of cloud. And so, Dora
had a lot of research into this idea of
like is the cloud and public cloud going
to help organizations? And through that
research, we were able to identify that
it wasn&#39;t whether or not you were using
cloud, but rather how you were using
cloud. And really, we we&#39;ve evolved that
that sort of thinking into this idea of
flexible infrastructure. So when you
have flexible infrastructure, teams tend
to do better than teams without that
flexible infrastructure. And of course,
one of the ways to get flexible
infrastructure is through public cloud.
So we do maintain a good bit of
independence. It is true that this
year&#39;s report, the 2025 report is called
the state of AI assisted software
development. And this certainly we we
live and work within Google. So we hear
and our colleagues are pushing a lot of
AI and advancing the the
state-of-the-art there. At the same
time, so many people across the industry
are doing this. And so from a Dora
perspective, we really want to
understand how is AI impacting software
delivery? How is it impacting these
teams? And so this is actually the third
year that we&#39;ve looked into AI
progressively going deeper and deeper.
So there&#39;s there&#39;s it would be it would
sort of be false to say that there&#39;s
absolutely no influence. There&#39;s
certainly influence but we do remain
fairly independent from Google cloud.
&gt;&gt; So before we get into the AI report
itself or reports because there have
been two of them now I want to ask you a
sort of more general question which is
something that I&#39;ve seen a bit in my own
consulting practice and it has to do
with the full door metrics.
&gt;&gt; The these are I think quite well
understood. Obviously this particular
question is somewhat anecdotal but it&#39;s
I&#39;m interested to know if it&#39;s something
you see as well. So I&#39;ve had a couple of
clients who were having you know sort of
team performance issues. They&#39;d adopted
the door metrics but they then seemed
very unclear as to what improvements to
make like where to focus. So they could
see what the metrics were telling them
if you like but they weren&#39;t then doing
the next bit which was sort of making a
hypothesis and doing doing some sort of
validation if you like. And obviously
there&#39;s a lot that&#39;s very context
specific here because if you&#39;re a young
team you probably want to be looking at
different things. if you&#39;re I don&#39;t know
a huge team in a bank or something but I
wondered if you could give if first of
all is that something you&#39;ve you&#39;ve seen
yourself and if it is do you have any
kind of general advice for people? Yes,
it is certainly something that I&#39;ve seen
and in fact this is something that over
time the research you know has has
continued to evolve and so while you
mentioned the four Dora metrics I&#39;m
really sort of excited maybe I don&#39;t
know if excited is the right term but I
I&#39;m happy to share that four have
actually become five in fact for the
past two years we&#39;ve looked at five
different metrics for software delivery
performance as before these metrics fall
under two sort of high level factors
throughput and stability. On the
throughput side, we have three measures
that we look at. Your lead time for
changes, so how long does it take for a
change to go from committed to running
in the production environment? Your
deployment frequency, how frequently are
you updating that production
environment? And your failed deployment
recovery time. So when something goes
off on a deployment, how long does it
take you to get that deployment back to
working? And on the stability side, we
have your change failure rate. And this
is a measure of how many deployments
require immediate intervention.
Something has gone wrong. We need humans
to inter intervene on these deployments.
And then finally, our fifth metric, and
this is the newest one, is your
deployment rework rate. So when you make
a deployment and have to rework that
deployment in some way, whether that&#39;s,
you know, maybe you&#39;re doing an
unplanned deployment to recover from
some failure, that would be considered
rework. And so that th those measures,
those five measures taken together,
there&#39;s a couple of really interesting
things about them. First, they can be
used for any type of software that
you&#39;re shipping into production or
making available to your users. And
second, we often times think of
throughput and stability as trade-offs
of one another, but over the years, over
the decade plus of this research, we&#39;ve
shown that they aren&#39;t trade-offs, but
rather they tend to move together. So
teams are either either have fast
throughput and high stability or low
throughput and low stability. Of course,
we probably want the the former, not the
latter. We want to be able to move fast
and move in a way that is very stable.
Now, when it comes to your question, how
do we go from really understanding what
these metrics are measuring, what do we
do with this once we understand exactly
how things are going? Well, this is
another thing where it&#39;s really
important to think about these metrics
kind of serve two purposes. One purpose
is that these metrics in our data and
our research. We&#39;ve shown them to be
leading indicators for the outcomes that
teams care about. Things like
organizational performance and
well-being for the people on your team.
But these metrics are also lagging
indicators for the capabilities and
conditions that you have on your team.
For example, you need a climate for
learning. you need fast flow and fast
feedback in order to improve those
metrics. Now, with the DORA model and
through our research, we investigate
those capabilities over time to really
understand how do those capabilities
relate to software delivery performance
and we find things like documentation
quality, streamlining change approval
processes, continuous integration, all
of these contribute to better software
delivery performance. So the thing that
I really encourage teams to do is to use
the DORA model of these capabilities
together with these metrics. Use the
metrics to get a baseline for how is
your team doing today and then take into
consideration the capabilities and kind
of run a quick assessment across those
capabilities. Where does our team have a
weakness or an opportunity to improve
and then go run an experiment. You know
take Dora&#39;s findings as your hypothesis.
A a good example of this, Dora has found
that as you get better at continuous
integration, that improves software
delivery performance. So now maybe your
team isn&#39;t practicing continuous
integration or has opportunities to
improve it. Sit down and write that
hypothesis. We believe that by improving
our continuous integration practices,
we&#39;re going to see software delivery
performance improved as measured by
these metrics and as a result of that,
we&#39;re going to see happier customers.
Now that you&#39;ve got that hypothesis
written down, you can go back and start
improving or changing how you do
continuous integration and you can
validate that hypothesis. You can
validate our research in the context of
your team. And I think that&#39;s what&#39;s
super important is that you&#39;re taking
our research and contextualizing it for
your team within your organization.
&gt;&gt; That&#39;s a fantastic answer. Thank you.
So, um, it would be remiss of me not to
start diving into the AI stuff at this
point. So there was a rather headline
grabbing finding in the 2024 Dora report
which basically said that the more AI
was used the worse both stability and
throughput became. So more roll backs
and so on. And [snorts] obviously that&#39;s
essentially what we&#39;ve been optimizing
for most of the last 20 years. So it&#39;s
not a great finding. Now I should say
the 2025 report kind of suggests the
opposite. But I was interested if you
could maybe give us some context there.
what tell talk about that finding a bit
and what maybe what it&#39;s telling us.
&gt;&gt; Yeah, for sure. So, in 2024, we did see
in fact that as teams are adopting more
AI, both throughput and stability were
falling off. There was a small reversal
in 2025 as teams are adapting to AI. We
see throughput is actually improving as
you use more AI, but we still see high
levels of instability when you use more
AI. So when I think about this, I I I
think there are probably a couple of
different explanations. The first
explanation I think is is probably the
simplest and that is we&#39;re using a new
tool and using new processes as we&#39;re
developing software. Anytime you
introduce something new, we should
expect to see some fall off in
performance as we learn how to adapt to
this new technology or this new way of
working and how that might improve
overall performance. But I think the
other thing that is really interesting
here and another hypothesis that I have
is that as an industry, one of the
biggest ways and first ways that we&#39;ve
used AI within software development is
to use it to generate more code. Now,
when you think about the entire software
delivery process, everything from having
an idea to getting that idea into
customers in a tangible way within your
within your systems. It is rarely the
case that writing code is the bottleneck
in that process. And yet we&#39;ve we put a
lot of emphasis on AI to help us
generate or author more code. Your
bottlenecks are usually downstream from
that. And we kind of know that in any
system that you&#39;re working in, if
there&#39;s a flow of work that goes through
that system, somewhere there&#39;s a
constraint. And if you make an
improvement that&#39;s not at that
constraint, you&#39;re probably not
improving the overall system
performance. In fact, you may be harming
it. And so in this case in 2024 I think
that&#39;s what we were seeing generating
more code and generating code faster but
the mechanisms the feedback mechanisms
the flow mechanisms that allow that code
to get into the production environment
hadn&#39;t adapted are weren&#39;t able to sort
of account for or handle this new
onslaught of additional code. I think
that&#39;s a big reason why we&#39;re seeing
that and we&#39;re starting to see as I
mentioned some of that change now in
2025. Yeah, I I that&#39;s kind of very much
chimes with my thinking on it. And
actually, you know, I said at the top of
this show, I&#39;ve been in this industry a
long time and I feel like we&#39;ve beaten
this to death. Like we&#39;ve been over and
over and over again the idea that typing
is the hard bit and it&#39;s not. which is
why, you know, measuring lines of code
or GitHub commits or any of those things
are just terrible, terrible metrics
because, you know, as an indicator of
performance and a they&#39;re very gameable,
but b they don&#39;t really tell you
anything. And it kind of feels a bit to
me like we&#39;re going round another of
these leaps of optimizing individual
developer productivity, but doing that
at the expense of the system as a whole,
which seems to me to be, you know, I&#39;d
have thought by now we&#39;d have got away
with from that, but but apparently not.
&gt;&gt; Yeah. And I I I think that systems
thinking is so so important. I mean, you
could even you could you could lay the
same criticism against those software
delivery performance metrics. That&#39;s not
actually telling you whether or not
you&#39;re delivering business value or
customer value. And I I would agree with
that. But our research has shown that as
you improve software delivery
performance, you&#39;re also improving those
outcomes that matter. And so I challenge
every organization that&#39;s using these to
put those software delivery metrics side
by side with the business metrics that
they actually care about. You should see
them moving together. And when you
don&#39;t, that&#39;s cause for investigation,
cause for inquiry. Let&#39;s go figure out
why these aren&#39;t moving together and see
what can we do to change that.
&gt;&gt; So in the most recent report, and also I
saw you emphasize this in your keynote
as well, you talked about AI as an
amplifier. So can you unpack that a bit
for me? What does that mean? Yeah, I I
really think that AI and what we&#39;re kind
of seeing in the data is that it
amplifies sort of the underlying systems
that exist within organizations.
Organizations where software changes can
flow easily and there&#39;s good feedback
mechanisms along the way. AI tends to
amplify or speed up that that flow of
software. In in in contrast to that
where you have organizations that are
disconnected or there&#39;s a lot of
friction and getting changes through
your system, AI tends to sort of
highlight here&#39;s where the pains are.
I&#39;ll give you a really good example like
a crisp example that we&#39;ve actually been
researching for a couple of years. If we
go back to 2023, which was really one of
the first years that we investigated AI,
one of the findings that we had in that
year was that the code review process
was often a bottleneck for teams. And
this was with or without AI. But we
found that those teams that had faster
code reviews had about 50% better
software delivery performance. It was
kind of a onetoone mapping. As you
improve code review process and speed,
software delivery speed also improved.
now in inject AI to help us create more
code. If we haven&#39;t addressed code
review as a bottleneck, we&#39;re now
sending more code into that code review
process. And so that&#39;s going to feel
even more painful. That&#39;s a great
example of AI amplifying some pain that
we have there. The code reviews are
actually going to take longer. They&#39;re
going to get slower because we&#39;re
generating more code. Contrast that with
somewhere an organization that has a
good highquality fast feedback process
when it comes to code reviews and AI is
going to help us improve that. And in
fact, what this may lead you to as an
organization is understanding that maybe
we&#39;ll get more benefit out of using AI
in the code review process than we will
in the code authoring process. That&#39;s
one of the sort of ways that you can
contextualize these findings within your
own team. What would you say are some of
the things that technology organizations
need to get into in place before they
try and scale an AI adoption?
&gt;&gt; Yeah, this is a really good question and
it&#39;s one of the sort of research
questions that we had. Like I said
earlier in our in our research program,
we we looked at the cloud and it wasn&#39;t
that you were using the cloud but rather
how you were using the cloud. So this
year we wanted to understand what
capabilities really enhance AI adoption
and the impacts that AI adoption is
having. And so we investigated a bunch
of capabilities based on the hypotheses
that we had. But we narrowed it down to
about seven capabilities which we are
now calling the DORA AI capabilities
model. These capabilities and conditions
when mapped together with heavy AI
adoption, these capabilities amplify
that adoption on the outcomes that you
care about. Things like reducing
friction, things like better product
performance and so forth. So the seven
capabilities that we have, and I&#39;m going
to do this off the top of my head, so
forgive me if I stut stutter here just a
little bit, but the first is a clear and
communicated stance on how and where and
when AI can be used within your
organization. This is really important
to have. The others are having a good
data ecosystem. Kind of following the uh
old adage, you know, garbage in, garbage
out. The AI has to have access to good
data. That data has to be well
connected. Which leads us to our third,
which is AI having access to that
internal data. Fourth, we have strong
version control practices. You know, if
AI is generating a lot of code for us,
we probably want to be checking in those
changes very frequently so that when
something goes wrong, we can we can rely
on the roll back capabilities that
version control gives us. Another is
again sort of a classic thing that we&#39;ve
learned within software engineering and
that&#39;s working in smaller batches.
Instead of taking out a big change, what
we do as engineers is we take large
changes and break them down into small
changes. Doing so helps the AI have even
stronger impact on the things that we
care about. Number six is a user centric
focus. We aren&#39;t using AI for AI. We&#39;re
using it to support the needs of our
users to help delight them. And then
finally, having a good internal platform
in place. We see that again as an
amplifier of the AI adoption that
happens within an organization. So those
are the seven DORA AI capabilities. We
expect that those are going to change
over time. Just like our four software
delivery metrics are now five. We expect
that these capabilities are going to
change and evolve over time as we learn
more both as an industry and as a
research program. [snorts]
&gt;&gt; And it&#39;s worth saying I think some of
the I mean obviously some of those are
very software specific but I think some
of those apply equally well outside of a
software organization. I mean the having
a clear AI policy, having a clear AI
stance is something that every
organization that&#39;s adopting AI in any
context, that&#39;s a thing that you need in
place. I&#39;m I&#39;m I&#39;m I&#39;m thrilled to see
this. It&#39;s it&#39;s sort of validating a lot
of a lot of ideas that I think people
have had and and and giving real weight
to them. And I think that&#39;s tremendous.
&gt;&gt; That&#39;s awesome. Yeah. And and to your
point, you know, when we look at AI
adoption, we are looking at it beyond
just using AI to write code or within
the software delivery practice, we we
are really looking at AI across the
organization.
&gt;&gt; So earlier [clears throat] on you
mentioned the importance of
documentation and this has been a lovely
thing for me because it&#39;s been a drum
I&#39;ve beaten for most of my career and I
have to tell you at times it&#39;s a lonely
drum. So that you know having the last
four years being able to point to Dora
and go look it turns out that
documentation quality does actually have
an influence on software delivery
performance has been nice. In the most
recent report you say that AI adoption
helps improve that. And I&#39;m going to be
honest and say I find that quite
surprising. So as an editor all of my
experience has kind of been the
opposite. Like anything that&#39;s very
obviously written by a large language
model is just painfully difficult to
edit. And it&#39;s partly because it breaks
your heristics. You know, you can
normally tell when a a human being is
going off the edge of their knowledge
and oh, I need to fact check that a bit
more. You know, like well, as with a
large language model, it&#39;s super hard to
tell. But anyway, can you help my
understanding of this? How are people
using AI for documentation? How&#39;s that
why is it helping? Why is it improving
quality? Do you
&gt;&gt; Yeah, it&#39;s it&#39;s it&#39;s really interesting.
And documentation, like you said, is
something that we&#39;ve looked at for many
many years. We have a saying around
Dora, documentation is like sunshine. It
really unlocks a lot of the things that
matter to technologydriven organizations
and technologydriven teams. And you&#39;re
also correct that in in 2024 in
particular, what we saw was that as you
increase your usage of AI, documentation
quality tends to improve. Now, it&#39;s
really interesting because we of course
we aren&#39;t asking about documentation
quantity, right? You don&#39;t measure
documentation by the pound. That&#39;s not
what matters. We we do ask, you know,
survey questions that get to the quality
of the documentation. Survey questions
like if there&#39;s a problem, do you reach
for the documentation? That&#39;s a good
indicator that you have good quality
documentation. And while we saw
documentation like those quality signals
improving as you use more AI, we have a
couple of hypotheses around those. first
and first and foremost, maybe you&#39;re
using AI to generate more documentation
and and perhaps it is helping improve
some of the documentation quality. I&#39;ll
speak from personal experience. I
pointed an LLM at a a project that I was
working with that had no getting started
documentation. I said, &quot;Write a doc that
helps a developer get started in this
particular project.&quot; And it did a fair
